articles.title: Are India and Indonesia Leaving the Non-Aligned Movement Behind?
articles.excerpt: When Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited Jakarta last month, the joint statement issued by India and Indonesia addressed almost every major strategic issue facing Asia. It highlighted the Indo-Pacific, BRICS, ASEAN, maritime security, artificial intelligence, critical minerals, resilient supply chains, and cooperation among the Global South. Yet there was no reference to the Non Aligned Movement (NAM), despite India and Indonesia being among its founding members and the leaders whose cooperation at the 1955 Bandung Conference helped lay its intellectual foundations. The NAM was similarly absent from the joint statement issued during President Prabowo Subianto’s visit to India in January 2025. The disappearance of the NAM offers a window into how two of Asia’s most important middle powers now understand strategic autonomy. Rather than signaling the abandonment of non-alignment, the same principles are increasingly pursued through a different set of institutions, partnerships, and diplomatic priorities. India and Indonesia have long occupied a unique place in the history of postcolonial diplomacy. The Bandung Conference articulated principles of sovereignty, anti-colonialism, peaceful coexistence, and independent foreign policy that later shaped the establishment of the NAM in 1961. During the Cold War, these ideas provided newly independent states with a framework for resisting pressure to align with either Washington or Moscow while asserting a greater voice in international affairs. But the strategic environment that gave rise to non-alignment no longer exists. The central challenge facing Asian middle powers today is not simply avoiding military blocs. It is preserving policy autonomy while navigating an increasingly complex landscape shaped by great power competition, economic interdependence, technological rivalry, and overlapping regional institutions. articles.title: Has Life in North Korea Changed Since 2013?
articles.excerpt: Last month, as I launched my new book “Witness to North Korea,” conversations with Wall Street Beijing Bureau Chief Jonathan Cheng and NK News’ Alannah Hill brought up one important question: is this memoir of my three years living and working as the United Nations Resident Coordinator in the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) still relevant to the North Korea of today? I wrote this book for anyone wishing to understand, as Stimson Center Fellow Frank Aum wrote, “what it actually means to engage with the DPRK – not in the abstract language of policy briefs, but through the granular, often maddening, reality of day-to-day diplomacy and humanitarian work.” This question of continued relevance between what I observed then and the country today is a valid one. After all, I left Pyongyang in 2013 – and yes, things in the country have changed since my departure. Some North Korea experts talk of a rising middle class with cash to spare, of one mobile phone subscriber for every three North Koreans, of ski resorts – all thanks to the phenomena of marketization and monetization changing the up-to-now closed economy and forcing the hand of the North Korean regime to open to international trade. Another thing has changed: data has become even harder to obtain. In 2020, North Korea used the COVID-19 pandemic to deny entry to several EU-member countries that had kept an embassy in Pyongyang and to most of the international community’s assistance programs. These embassies and resident U.N. agencies, as well as most international NGOs, have not yet returned. The U.N. population census remains, to this day, an essential source of quality data about North Korean society. Sadly, there has not been such an exercise since I left 13 years ago. My discussions with U.N. officials and humanitarian organizations point, today, to a continuation of the underlying problems that I describe in my book, which continue to shape the lives of ordinary North Koreans. articles.title: When the World Stops Fearing the Bomb
articles.excerpt: Terumi Tanaka was 13 when on one fine day the sky above Nagasaki was suddenly flooded with blinding white glare; “a blazing inferno” he would recall years later. At 97 now, he still carries memories of sitting next to the window. His home was hit suddenly by a flash, then thunder, followed by an unbearable silence. Within moments, his city was reduced to ash. “It was literally hell,” he said in his eyewitness account. With the average age of the hibakusha (atomic bombing survivors) reaching 87, there will soon be no one left to provide such first-person testimony. As humanity loses these eyewitnesses — 91,105 left as of March 2026 — we are also losing our moral compass. As the world commemorates the 81st anniversary of the dropping of atomic bombs on Japan, a cruel irony is fast unfolding in front of our eyes. The generation that witnessed the Hiroshima and Nagasaki bombings is fading away just as the world rediscovers the strategic significance of nuclear weapons — and loses sight of the human suffering such weapons embody. For decades, the horrors of Hiroshima and Nagasaki had imposed an invisible restraint on policymakers. Nuclear weapons were tolerated, but never celebrated. The nuclear taboo — non-possession, non-transfer, and non-use of nuclear weapons — was assumed to be universal and robust. Today, deterrence has displaced disarmament as the dominant concern. Even before the last hibakusha leave this earth, the world is turning its back on their warnings. The Return of the Bomb The nine nuclear-armed states possess 12,241 nuclear warheads, with nearly 9,614 retained in military stockpiles. This is certainly better than 70,300 warheads in 1986 when Russia and the United States possessed more than 90 percent of the world’s nuclear bombs. Driven by their detente of 1970s and the end of Cold War from late 1980s, the Soviet-U.S. (and later Russia-U.S.) arms control agreements had really shrunk their arsenals. articles.title: Why Asia Is More Enthusiastic About AI Than the West

Credit: Depositphotos We are living in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). AI dominates the headlines, spreads its influence into all spheres of life, and is increasingly seen as vital to the economic growth and national security of nations. The use of large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and Claude have become ubiquitous in daily life. Needless to say, the increased spread of AI — and its impact on relationships, employment, and other facets of society — has provoked trepidation among many. articles.title: China’s World AI Cooperation Organization Agenda

articles.title: 15 Months After Massacre at Pahalgam, Terrorists Target Non-local Civilians Again in Kashmir
articles.excerpt: A year of relative calm in the Kashmir valley was shattered on July 31 when terrorists opened fire on two non-local laborers at a brick kiln in Kilam village of South Kashmir’s Kulgam district. The two laborers were migrants from the central Indian state of Chhattisgarh. The attack at Kulgam has triggered panic among tens of thousands of laborers from India’s poorer northern states, who come to the Kashmir valley every year between March and November to work on construction sites, road projects, brick kilns, and apple orchards. The July 31 killings prompted some of them to return home. The Kulgam attack came close on the heels of the killing of a Jammu and Kashmir (J&K) police constable at a busy market in Anantnag district. The attacks have raised concern over the return of terrorism to the Kashmir valley. Indeed, the incident at Kulgam is the first targeted killing of non-local civilians by terrorists since April 22, 2025, when 26 men, all civilians, were shot dead at Pahalgam; 25 of them were from outside J&K and one was a Kashmiri pony ride operator, who tried to stop the shooting. There had been no attacks on civilians since then; the bloodletting over the past fortnight broke that lull. The killings at Kulgam came days before the seventh anniversary of New Delhi’s abrogation of J&K’s autonomy. It was on August 5, 2019, that the Narendra Modi government announced the revocation of Article 370 and Article 35A – a unilateral action that was hugely unpopular in J&K. articles.excerpt: Asia Defense | Security | East Asia South Korea’s army thought they were locked on to a North Korean UAV. It actually belonged to the U.S. Marine Corps. U.S. Marines employ a Stalker VXE30 Unmanned Aerial System during a Combined Arms Live-Fire Exercise at Rodriguez Live-Fire Complex, South Korea, March 5, 2026. Credit: U.S. Marine Corps photo by Cpl. Rodney Frye On July 30, air defense units along South Korea’s front line in Paju, Gyeonggi Province, detected an unidentified aerial track on a thermal observation device (TOD) and local air defense radars. Assessing the object as a potential airborne threat, the South Korean Army Ground Operations Command immediately issued “Durumi,” a high-alert air defense posture triggered in response to suspected enemy unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) incursions. For 90 minutes, anti-aircraft gun systems and attack helicopters were placed on emergency standby in a state of high tension. While a friendly-fire incident was narrowly averted, the implications are profound. Severe vulnerabilities exist in both asset management and inter-ally command-and-control communication mechanisms along the Korean Peninsula. A closer look at the sequence of events underscores systemic operational flaws. Prior to the exercise, U.S. forces had notified South Korean military counterparts of their flight plans and formally dispatched official documentation. Yet, this critical information stalled at the working level within the South Korean military bureaucracy; it was neither briefed upward to senior command nor disseminated down to frontline units. articles.title: When Small States Practice Buddhist Diplomacy
articles.excerpt: As strategic competition between China and India intensifies, Buddhism has become an increasingly visible instrument of foreign policy. China has positioned itself as a center of Mahayana Buddhist civilization, sponsoring international Buddhist forums, restoring sacred sites, and weaving Buddhist heritage into its Belt and Road Initiative. India, the birthplace of Buddhism, has promoted its own Buddhist heritage by expanding pilgrimage circuits and lending sacred relics abroad. The focus on China and India obscures a quieter, yet equally significant, story. Buddhist diplomacy is being practiced not only by Asia’s largest powers, but also by two of its smallest states: Bhutan and Singapore. The cases of Bhutan and Singapore demonstrate how small states can pursue Buddhist diplomacy under different conditions. Their limited geopolitical weight and lack of great power status have encouraged them to cultivate influence through cultural networks and regional cooperation. Bhutan, the world’s only official Vajrayana Buddhist kingdom, is a small, landlocked Himalayan state that has placed Buddhist values at the heart of both its domestic governance and its engagement with the world. This approach owes much to the vision of the Fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, who developed Gross National Happiness not simply as an alternative measure of development, but as a strategy for reconciling modernization with the preservation of Bhutan’s Buddhist culture and national identity. For a small state situated between India and China, this fusion of Buddhist values and development also served a strategic purpose, turning cultural distinctiveness into a means of safeguarding sovereignty while giving Bhutan an international profile far beyond its size. articles.title: China’s ‘Internet Addiction’ Schools Are Now Locking Up Adults
articles.excerpt: In March, a 21-year-old music student in Beijing arrived at an apartment complex to teach a piano lesson. Waiting for her were her father, her aunt, and two employees of a private disciplinary institution. Her relatives told her the strangers were police officers investigating a family matter. Instead, they forced her into a vehicle, confiscated her phone, and drove her hundreds of miles to an institution in Henan province, where she spent the next 11 days. According to Southern People Weekly, her parents objected to her romantic relationship and believed their once-obedient daughter had become difficult to manage. Public reporting indicates that this institution charged 26,800 yuan (around $4,000) for six months or 36,800 yuan for a year, including room and board. Another investigation by Jiemian News found adults as old as 33 living alongside teenagers in one behavioral correction school. These institutions emerged during the 2000s, amid national anxiety over youth “internet addiction.” Many gained notoriety for military-style discipline and physical punishment before public criticism pushed the industry to rebrand as family education centers, behavioral intervention programs, or youth development organizations. articles.title: Russia’s New Move in the Kuril Dispute
articles.excerpt: The planned naming of a disputed Kuril island after Richard Sorge is the latest example of Russia strengthening its control over the features. It is part of a decade-long effort by Moscow to use commemoration to reinforce its claim regardless of Tokyo’s protest. On July 28, the Sakhalin branch of the Russian Geographical Society announced the future placement of a plaque for Sorge, a Soviet intelligence officer, on an uninhabited island in the Lesser Kurils. Moscow is expected to rename the island after Sorge soon. The announcement drew attention in Japan given the island’s location and Sorge’s legacy. The island is part of the disputed Southern Kurils, which Japan calls the Northern Territories. The Kuril Islands stretch from Hokkaido to the Kamchatka Peninsula and provide Russia with protected access from the Sea of Okhotsk to the Pacific. Soviet forces occupied the islands in 1945, just before Japan’s surrender ended World War II. Japan still claims the southernmost four features: Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan, and the Habomai Islands. More than 80 years later, the dispute remains unresolved. Map of the Northern Territories of Japan (Kuril Islands). Wikimedia Commons. Disguised as a German journalist, Sorge led a successful espionage network for Moscow in Tokyo from 1933 until his arrest in October 1941. A close friendship with German Ambassador Eugen Ott and partnership with Japanese journalist Ozaki Hotsumi gave Sorge unmatched access. Ott’s confidence gave him insights into the German-Japan alliance. Ozaki’s ties to Prime Minister Konoe Fumimaro’s inner circle gave Sorge access to information from the highest levels of the Japanese government. The network layered political information with military activity to validate details, increasing the reliability of their reporting. articles.title: Germany’s Deportation of an Afghan Without Criminal Record Sets a New Precedent

articles.title: How Aging Populations Are Transforming Police Work Across Asia
articles.excerpt: Features | Society | East Asia In East Asia’s graying societies, police are becoming the “catch-all” agency for managing aging, like dementia-related wandering. Credit: Shutterstock About one-third of East Asia’s population is projected to be 60 or older by 2050, making it the world’s fastest-aging region. Public debates about population aging have largely centered on its effects on democratic governance, economic growth, pension sustainability, healthcare, urban planning, and housing policy. Yet one area remains notably underdiscussed: policing. Across graying societies, police are becoming the “catch-all” agency for managing aging as their roles and workloads have expanded in unprecedented ways. Police officers frequently mobilize to search for missing seniors and answer late-night calls from those who are confused or disoriented. As AI-powered scams become increasingly common, officers are playing a growing role as educators and protectors, helping older adults recognize and avoid financial fraud. They are often the first on the scene when older adults experience falls, heart attacks, strokes, or other medical emergencies. They are also on the front lines of social service delivery, responding to mounting cases of elder abuse or neglect and routinely conducting welfare checks as social isolation and kinship erosion damage mental health. Furthermore, increasing traffic incidents involving elderly drivers have prompted the police to engage in driver safety campaigns and to identify and report at-risk older drivers. Beneath this expanding portfolio of aging-related police work lies a revolution in policing and governance more broadly.
